implementation_notes: The library implements the pattern: mixing PackratParsers into a parser turns each memoized production into a lazy val ... : PackratParser[T] (instead of def ... : Parser[T]), and the memo table is attached to the input - PackratReader wraps an underlying reader and caches results in a mutable.HashMap[(Parser, Position), MemoEntry], i.e. keyed by exactly (rule, position), with failures stored as entries and left recursion supported by the Warth/Douglass/Millstein seed-growing algorithm that the trait cites alongside Ford. What replaces the classic structure is that there is no table of your own to size, key or clear: phrase wraps the input in a PackratReader and the rules only change their declaration form. Because the cache hangs off the input, memoization is per parse by construction, and the library states that memoizing and ordinary parsers can be mixed freely - the documented escape for stateful productions.
code_sketch:
import scala.util.parsing.combinator._

object Expr extends JavaTokenParsers with PackratParsers {
  lazy val expr: PackratParser[Int] =        // lazy val, not def: memoized by (rule, position)
    (expr ~ ("+" ~> term)) ^^ { case a ~ b => a + b } | term
  lazy val term: PackratParser[Int] = rep1(digit) ^^ (_.mkString.toInt)
}

val in: Input = new PackratReader(new lexical.Scanner("1+2+3"))
phrase(Expr.expr)(in)                        // phrase wraps the input for you
pitfalls: Only productions declared as lazy val ... : PackratParser[T] are memoized; a def or a plain Parser[T] rule is evaluated without the cache, so mixing is allowed but you must know which rules still pay the exponential path.
The cache lives on the PackratReader, so input that is not wrapped (or an entry point other than phrase) gets no memoization at all.
Stateful productions remain unsound under a position key: keep state-reading rules out of the memoized set, as the library's mixing rule allows.
The reader retains the whole input and every parse result for its lifetime; drop readers instead of keeping them for incremental work you are not doing.
